All reagents and samples used according manufacturer protocols by thawed completely, mixed (by pipetting or gentle vortexing). 2.2 Study population and sample collection: The present study entitled “Prevalence and Genomic Analysis of Circulating Dengue Virus Serotypes in Karnataka, India” will be conducted in the Department of Microbiology, BMCRI Medical College, Bengaluru. For a period of 12 months i.e., from January to December 2024. A total of 825. Serum samples were collected from male and female patients of all ages with clinical features of dengue disease visiting Department of Microbiology, BMCRI Medical College, Hospital, Bengaluru were included in this study. Figure 1: Flow Chart of study Page: 2 1 3 4 Molecular Detection and Sero-Prevalence Study of Circulating Dengue Virus in Karnataka During 2024 IJDDT, Volume 16 Issue 86s, 2026 2.3 Collection of the clinical samples and Ethical approval for this study: The blood samples of about 5 ml were collected from symptomatic patients in a sterile clot activator vacutainer, along with clinical and demographic information from tertiary care hospitals located in various district of Karnataka, India. The blood samples used in this study were collected during dengue outbreak in Karnataka, between January -2024 to December 2024.This study was undertaken after obtaining the ethical clearance (Ref.No: BMCRI/EC/64/24) from the Ethics Committee of the Bangalore Medical College and Research Institute, Bengaluru. And the present study entitled “Prevalence Analysis of Circulating Dengue Virus Serotypes in Karnataka, India” was conducted in the Department of Microbiology, BMCRI Medical College, Bengaluru. Before collecting the blood samples, informed consent was obtained from the participants. The samples were transported at 4 0C to the laboratory. Serum from the blood samples was separated and stored at - 80 0C until further analysis. All serum samples were screened seroprevalence studies by using Immunological tests ELISA by detecting DENV NS1 antigen and IgM antibody Kit (Standard Diagnostic Inc., Korea) according to the manual as well Molecular techniques like Dengue Qualitative REAL TIME PCR and Dengue Serotyping REAL TIME PCR. 2.4 Human serological testing: 2.4.1 Detection of dengue virus: Study on the molecular detection and Sero-prevalence of circulating dengue viruses typically involves two main components: molecular detection methods to identify the presence of the virus in biological samples, and sero-prevalence studies to determine the level of antibodies against the virus in a population (Mustafa et al., 2023). ELISATwo different ELISA kits were used for the detection of NS1Ag and IgM in all the samples: 1. ELISA assay for NS1Ag: dengue NS1Ag was detected using an InBios dengue NS1Ag ELISA kit according to the manufacturer’s instructions. 2.5. ELISA assay for IgM: dengue IgM antibodies were detected using an IgM MAC ELISA kit by NIV Pune as per the instructions provided. 2.5 Dengue Qualitative RT-PCR & Dengue Serotyping RT- PCR: Dengue Qualitative RT-PCR & Dengue Serotyping RT- PCR Detailed sociodemographic information of patients i.e., age, gender, clinical features and geographical area were documented. RNA extraction: A QIAamp Viral RNA Mini kit (Qiagen) was used to extract viral RNA from serum samples of dengue-positive patients, as per the manufacturer’s instructions. cDNA synthesis: As per the manufacturer’s instructions, reverse transcriptase PCR was used to synthesize cDNA from the extracted RNA using the Thermo Scientific RevertAid First Strand cDNA Synthesis Kit. PCR assay for serotyping: PCR was performed in 350 dengue NS1Ag ELISA-positive samples using a primer set defined by Lanciotti et al . Briefly, we used 10 μl PCR master-mix 2× (Thermo Scientific), 1 μl forward primer (D1), 1 μl reverse primer (D2), 2 μl PCR-grade water and 6 μl cDNA; thermal-cycler conditions were 94 °C for 5 min, 94 °C for 30 s, 55 °C for 60 s and 72 °C for 120 s, 72 °C for 5 min and cooling at 4 °C. Serotypes DEN-1 to DEN-4 were detected by performing a second nested PCR using type- specific primers as defined by Lanciotti et al. (Table 1). The amplified product was then subjected to gel electrophoresis to analyze the result. 2.6 Statistical analysis: The collected data were checked, coded, and entered into graphed prism for analysis. Descriptive statistics were done and result was presented using text and frequency tables. 3. Results and Discussion: The present study entitled “Prevalence and Genomic Analysis of Circulating Dengue Virus Serotypes in Karnataka, India” will be conducted in the Department of Microbiology, BMCRI Medical College, Bengaluru. 3.1 Evaluation of samples through Immunological and Molecular Techniques: The samples collected were processed for further analysis. full_text: Article original Coïnfection paludisme-dengue en milieu pédiatrique au Centre Hospitalier Universitaire de Bogodogo, Ouagadougou (Burkina Faso) Malaria-dengue coinfection in a pediatric setting at Bogodogo University Hospital, Ouagadougou (Burkina Faso) Sawadogo Hamidou1,3, Simpore Bernadette2,3, Nombre Alassane2,3, Ilboudo Serge2, Bilgo Aimé2, Ouedraogo Solange2,3 1Centre Médical avec antenne chirurgicale (CMA) de Kossodo, Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso. 2Centre hospitalier universitaire de Bogodogo, Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso. 3Unité de Formation et de Recherche en Sciences de la Santé, Université Joseph Ki Zerbo (UJKZ), Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso. Correspondance : Sawadogo Hamidou — shamidou86@gmail.com DOI : https://doi.org/10.68500/bh.v1i2.13 Reçu : 18 juillet 2026 · Accepté : 28 septembre 2026 · Publié : 15 octobre 2026 Résumé Introduction. La coïnfection paludisme-dengue constitue un défi diagnostique et thérapeutique croissant en zone d’endémie, en particulier chez l’enfant. Cette étude visait à décrire les aspects épidémiologiques, cliniques, thérapeutiques et évolutifs de la coïnfection paludisme-dengue chez les enfants de moins de 15 ans au Centre Hospitalier Universitaire de Bogodogo (Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso). Patients et méthode. Il s’agissait d’une étude transversale, à collecte rétrospective, descriptive, incluant de façon exhaustive tous les enfants de moins de 15 ans ayant présenté une coïnfection paludisme-dengue dans le service de pédiatrie du CHU-Bogodogo du 1er janvier au 31 décembre 2024. Résultats. Trente-quatre enfants ont été inclus. L’âge moyen était de 7,62 ± 4,07 ans, avec une prédominance féminine (55,9 %). Le pic des admissions survenait en octobre-novembre. La fièvre (97,1 %), les céphalées (64,7 %) et les vomissements (61,8 %) dominaient le tableau clinique. La forme « paludisme grave associé à une dengue probable sans signe d’alerte » était la plus fréquente (35,3 %). Une anémie (44,1 %), une CRP élevée (91,2 %) et une cytolyse hépatique (38,2 %) étaient les principales anomalies biologiques. Tous les patients ont reçu un traitement antipaludique. L’évolution était favorable dans 88,2 % des cas, avec un taux de létalité de 8,8 %. Conclusion. La coïnfection paludisme-dengue représente un défi diagnostique et thérapeutique en milieu pédiatrique, où les présentations cliniques peuvent être atypiques et les complications rapidement graves. Un dépistage systématique et concomitant du paludisme et de la dengue chez l’enfant fébrile en zone endémique est nécessaire pour optimiser la prise en charge et réduire la morbi-mortalité. Mots-clés : Coïnfection, paludisme, dengue, pédiatrie, Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso Abstract Introduction. Malaria-dengue coinfection is an increasing diagnostic and therapeutic challenge in endemic areas, particularly in children. This study aimed to describe the epidemiological, clinical, therapeutic, and outcome features of malaria-dengue coinfection in children under 15 years at Bogodogo University Hospital (Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso). Patients and method. This was a retrospective, descriptive cross-sectional study including, exhaustively, all children under 15 years with malaria-dengue coinfection managed in the pediatric department of Bogodogo University Hospital from January 1 to December 31, 2024. Results. Thirty-four children were included. Mean age was 7.62 ± 4.07 years, with a female predominance (55.9%). Admissions peaked in October-November. Fever (97.1%), headache (64.7%), and vomiting (61.8%) were the predominant clinical features. Severe malaria associated with probable dengue without warning signs was the most frequent form (35.3%). Anemia (44.1%), elevated CRP (91.2%), and hepatic cytolysis (38.2%) were the main laboratory abnormalities. All patients received antimalarial treatment. Outcome was favorable in 88.2% of cases, with a case fatality rate of 8.8%. Conclusion. Malaria-dengue coinfection represents a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge in pediatric settings, where clinical presentations may be atypical and complications can rapidly become severe. Systematic and concurrent screening for malaria and dengue in febrile children in endemic areas is needed to optimize care and reduce morbidity and mortality. Keywords: Coinfection, malaria, dengue, pediatrics, Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso 1. Introduction La dengue est une arbovirose due à quatre sérotypes viraux (DENV-1 à DENV-4) de la famille des Flaviviridae, transmise à l’homme par la piqûre de moustiques femelles du genre Aedes, principalement Aedes aegypti [1]. Elle sévit en Afrique dans au moins 34 pays sur un mode endémo-épidémique [2] et se manifeste souvent par une fièvre isolée ou un syndrome pseudo-grippal pouvant être confondu à tort avec un paludisme [3], maladie fébrile parasitaire transmise par la piqûre de l’anophèle femelle. En zone d’endémie, ces deux affections peuvent coexister chez un même patient, réalisant une coïnfection paludisme-dengue qui représente un défi diagnostique et thérapeutique majeur, en particulier chez l’enfant, plus exposé aux formes graves [3]. À l’échelle mondiale, environ 390 millions de cas de dengue surviennent chaque année et 3,9 milliards de personnes réparties dans 128 pays sont exposées au risque d’infection [4]. En 2022, le Burkina Faso a notifié 11 656 675 cas de paludisme, dont 539 488 formes graves et 4 243 décès, parmi lesquels 2 925 enfants de moins de 5 ans [5]. Des données récentes issues de la région du Guiriko (Burkina Faso) rapportent une prévalence de la coïnfection paludisme-dengue variant de 7,1 % (coïnfection aiguë confirmée par RT-PCR) à 17,6 % (exposition dengue récente ou passée associée au paludisme), avec une recrudescence en fin de saison des pluies [6]. En Afrique, la prévalence de la coïnfection Plasmodium falciparum-dengue a significativement augmenté, passant de 0,9 % sur la période 2008-2013 à 5,5 % sur la période 2018-2021 [7]. Au Cameroun, un taux de coïnfection de 19,5 % a été rapporté chez l’enfant fébrile [8]. Au Burkina Faso, des taux respectifs de 12,9 % et 20,4 % ont été retrouvés par Yankéné [9] et par Ly [10]. Toutefois, les données pédiatriques concernant cette coïnfection demeurent rares dans notre pays. L’objectif de cette étude était de décrire les aspects épidémiologiques, cliniques, thérapeutiques et évolutifs de la coïnfection paludisme-dengue chez les enfants de moins de 15 ans pris en charge au CHU de Bogodogo (Ouagadougou) du 1er janvier au 31 décembre 2024, afin de contribuer à l’amélioration de leur prise en charge. 2. Patients et méthode L’étude s’est déroulée dans le service de pédiatrie médicale du Centre Hospitalier Universitaire de Bogodogo (CHU-B), structure de troisième niveau de référence à Ouagadougou, comportant une unité des urgences pédiatriques, une unité d’hospitalisation d’une capacité de 30 lits et une unité de néonatologie. Il s’agissait d’une étude transversale, à collecte de données rétrospective, à visée descriptive, portant sur la période du 1er janvier au 31 décembre 2024. Tous les enfants de moins de 15 ans ayant présenté simultanément un paludisme et une dengue au cours de leur prise en charge dans le service durant la période d’étude ont été inclus de façon exhaustive. Étaient exclus les dossiers inexploitables, c’est-à-dire sans informations cliniques suffisantes, sans diagnostic précis ou sans évolution clinique précisée. Les données sociodémographiques, anthropométriques, cliniques, paracliniques, thérapeutiques et évolutives ont été recueillies à partir des dossiers médicaux à l’aide d’une fiche de collecte standardisée et anonyme, l’enquêteur n’utilisant que le numéro de dossier. Le paludisme grave était défini selon les critères de l’Organisation mondiale de la santé, et la dengue classée en dengue probable sans signe d’alerte, dengue probable avec signe(s) d’alerte, ou dengue sévère, conformément aux directives nationales de prise en charge de la dengue au Burkina Faso [1]. L’état de conscience était évalué par le score de Blantyre chez les enfants de moins de 3 ans et par le score de Glasgow au-delà de 3 ans. Les données ont été saisies et analysées avec le logiciel Epi Info dans sa version française 7.2.5.2, et Microsoft Excel 2016 pour la réalisation des tableaux. Les variables quantitatives ont été exprimées en moyenne ± écart-type, et les variables qualitatives en effectif et pourcentage. L’étude a reçu l’autorisation de la commission d’éthique du CHU-Bogodogo et des responsables des services concernés. La confidentialité des données a été assurée par l’anonymisation des fiches de collecte, l’identification des patients se limitant au numéro de dossier ; les données recueillies ont été exclusivement utilisées dans un but d’amélioration de la prise en charge des patients. 3. Résultats Caractéristiques sociodémographiques et cliniques Durant la période d’étude, 34 enfants répondaient aux critères d’inclusion, dont 67,6 % (n = 23) ont été pris en charge dans l’unité d’hospitalisation pédiatrique. L’âge moyen était de 7,62 ± 4,07 ans (extrêmes : 0 et 14 ans). Une prédominance féminine était observée (55,9 %, n = 19), avec un sex-ratio homme/femme de 0,79. La quasi-totalité des patients résidait à Ouagadougou (91,2 %, n = 31). La majorité des patients (91,2 %, n = 31) était référée, principalement depuis un centre de santé et de promotion sociale (CSPS) (44,1 %, n = 15). Le délai de consultation était compris entre 2 et 7 jours chez 58,8 % des patients (n = 20), et supérieur à 7 jours chez un seul patient (2,9 %). La fièvre constituait le principal motif de consultation (97,1 %, n = 33), suivie des céphalées (64,7 %, n = 22), des vomissements (61,8 %, n = 21) et des douleurs abdominales (44,1 %, n = 15) (Tableau I). Un antécédent médical était retrouvé chez 20,6 % des patients (n = 7), dominé par l’infection néonatale (57,1 % des antécédents, n = 4/7). La température corporelle moyenne était de 38,9 ± 0,6 °C. L’état général était mauvais chez la moitié des patients (50 %, n = 17) et l’état de conscience était perturbé chez 41,2 % d’entre eux (altéré : 14,7 %, n = 5 ; obnubilé : 26,5 %, n = 9). Les signes de gravité les plus fréquents étaient la léthargie (52,9 %, n = 18), les vomissements persistants (35,3 %, n = 12), la détresse respiratoire (23,5 %, n = 8), l’ictère (20,6 %, n = 7) et l’hémorragie spontanée (11,8 %, n = 4). Les associations IgM-IgG (8,8 %, n = 3) et NS1-IgG (5,9 %, n = 2) étaient plus rares, et le profil sérologique n’était pas renseigné chez 3 patients (8,8 %) (Figure 1). Une anémie était présente chez 44,1 % des patients (n = 15), sévère dans 5,9 % des cas (n = 2), avec un taux d’hémoglobine moyen de 8,72 ± 2 g/dl. Une hémoconcentration (hématocrite élevé) était notée chez 20,6 % (n = 7) et une leucopénie chez 5,9 % (n = 2) des patients. La CRP était élevée chez 91,2 % des patients (n = 31) et la procalcitonine était élevée chez 66,7 % des patients testés (8/12). Une cytolyse hépatique majeure (ALAT > 120 UI/L) était observée chez 38,2 % des patients (n = 13) et une insuffisance rénale aiguë chez 37,5 % des patients testés pour la créatininémie (6/16) (Tableau II). Diagnostic et prise en charge thérapeutique La forme la plus fréquente était l’association paludisme grave et dengue probable sans signe d’alerte (35,3 %, n = 12), suivie du paludisme grave associé à une dengue probable avec signe(s) d’alerte (32,4 %, n = 11) et du paludisme grave associé à une dengue sévère (14,7 %, n = 5) (Tableau III). Une transfusion de culot globulaire a été nécessaire chez 55,9 % des patients (n = 19) (Tableau IV). Évolution La durée d’hospitalisation était comprise entre 5 et 7 jours chez 41,2 % des patients (n = 14), entre 2 et 4 jours chez 29,4 % (n = 10) et entre 8 et 12 jours chez 29,4 % (n = 10). L’évolution était favorable, sans séquelle, chez 88,2 % des enfants (n = 30) ; 3 décès ont été enregistrés, soit un taux de létalité de 8,8 %. 4. Discussion Cette étude rétrospective, monocentrique, menée dans une structure publique de troisième référence, a pu exposer nos résultats à un biais de sélection lié à l’exclusion d’une partie de la patientèle prise en charge dans le secteur privé, ainsi qu’à des données manquantes inhérentes à l’exploitation de dossiers cliniques. Elle présente néanmoins l’intérêt d’associer les aspects épidémiologiques, cliniques, thérapeutiques et évolutifs de la coïnfection paludisme-dengue chez l’enfant, encore peu documentés dans notre pays. Notre étude comporte par ailleurs plusieurs limites propres au recueil rétrospectif des données à partir des dossiers cliniques. La confirmation du paludisme reposait sur la seule positivité de la goutte épaisse, sans recueil systématique de la densité parasitaire ni de l’espèce plasmodiale en cause, ce qui ne permet pas de vérifier a posteriori l’ensemble des critères de gravité de l’Organisation mondiale de la santé. La numération plaquettaire et le bilan de coagulation (TP/TCA), bien que pertinents dans le suivi de la dengue, de même que les données anthropométriques recueillies, n’ont pas été exploités dans cette analyse. Les modalités de recherche d’une preuve d’infection bactérienne (hémoculture, examen cytobactériologique des urines, foyer clinique) justifiant le recours élargi aux antibiotiques n’ont pas non plus été systématiquement documentées. Enfin, le devenir précis d’un patient sur les 34 inclus, la description individuelle des trois décès enregistrés, le recours effectif à une unité de soins intensifs pédiatriques et la justification de l’absence de transfusion plaquettaire n’ont pu être détaillés à partir des dossiers sources disponibles. Ces éléments mériteraient d’être documentés de façon prospective dans de futurs travaux. Aspects épidém…

Correspondance : Sawadogo Hamidou — shamidou86@gmail.com DOI : https://doi.org/10.68500/bh.v1i2.13 Reçu : 18 juillet 2026 · Accepté : 28 septembre 2026 · Publié : 15 octobre 2026 Résumé Introduction. La coïnfection paludisme-dengue constitue un défi diagnostique et thérapeutique croissant en zone d’endémie, en particulier chez l’enfant. Cette étude visait à décrire les aspects épidémiologiques, cliniques, thérapeutiques et évolutifs de la coïnfection paludisme-dengue chez les enfants de moins de 15 ans au Centre Hospitalier Universitaire de Bogodogo (Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso). Patients et méthode. Il s’agissait d’une étude transversale, à collecte rétrospective, descriptive, incluant de façon exhaustive tous les enfants de moins de 15 ans ayant présenté une coïnfection paludisme-dengue dans le service de pédiatrie du CHU-Bogodogo du 1er janvier au 31 décembre 2024. Résultats. Trente-quatre enfants ont été inclus. L’âge moyen était de 7,62 ± 4,07 ans, avec une prédominance féminine (55,9 %). Le pic des admissions survenait en octobre-novembre. La fièvre (97,1 %), les céphalées (64,7 %) et les vomissements (61,8 %) dominaient le tableau clinique. La forme « paludisme grave associé à une dengue probable sans signe d’alerte » était la plus fréquente (35,3 %). Une anémie (44,1 %), une CRP élevée (91,2 %) et une cytolyse hépatique (38,2 %) étaient les principales anomalies biologiques. Tous les patients ont reçu un traitement antipaludique. L’évolution était favorable dans 88,2 % des cas, avec un taux de létalité de 8,8 %. Conclusion. La coïnfection paludisme-dengue représente un défi diagnostique et thérapeutique en milieu pédiatrique, où les présentations cliniques peuvent être atypiques et les complications rapidement graves. Un dépistage systématique et concomitant du paludisme et de la dengue chez l’enfant fébrile en zone endémique est nécessaire pour optimiser la prise en charge et réduire la morbi-mortalité. Mots-clés : Coïnfection, paludisme, dengue, pédiatrie, Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso Abstract Introduction. Malaria-dengue coinfection is an increasing diagnostic and therapeutic challenge in endemic areas, particularly in children. This study aimed to describe the epidemiological, clinical, therapeutic, and outcome features of malaria-dengue coinfection in children under 15 years at Bogodogo University Hospital (Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso). Patients and method. This was a retrospective, descriptive cross-sectional study including, exhaustively, all children under 15 years with malaria-dengue coinfection managed in the pediatric department of Bogodogo University Hospital from January 1 to December 31, 2024. Results. Thirty-four children were included. Mean age was 7.62 ± 4.07 years, with a female predominance (55.9%). Admissions peaked in October-November. Fever (97.1%), headache (64.7%), and vomiting (61.8%) were the predominant clinical features. Severe malaria associated with probable dengue without warning signs was the most frequent form (35.3%). Anemia (44.1%), elevated CRP (91.2%), and hepatic cytolysis (38.2%) were the main laboratory abnormalities. All patients received antimalarial treatment. Outcome was favorable in 88.2% of cases, with a case fatality rate of 8.8%. Conclusion. Malaria-dengue coinfection represents a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge in pediatric settings, where clinical presentations may be atypical and complications can rapidly become severe. Systematic and concurrent screening for malaria and dengue in febrile children in endemic areas is needed to optimize care and reduce morbidity and mortality. Keywords: Coinfection, malaria, dengue, pediatrics, Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso 1. Introduction La dengue est une arbovirose due à quatre sérotypes viraux (DENV-1 à DENV-4) de la famille des Flaviviridae, transmise à l’homme par la piqûre de moustiques femelles du genre Aedes, principalement Aedes aegypti [1]. Elle sévit en Afrique dans au moins 34 pays sur un mode endémo-épidémique [2] et se manifeste souvent par une fièvre isolée ou un syndrome pseudo-grippal pouvant être confondu à tort avec un paludisme [3], maladie fébrile parasitaire transmise par la piqûre de l’anophèle femelle. En zone d’endémie, ces deux affections peuvent coexister chez un même patient, réalisant une coïnfection paludisme-dengue qui représente un défi diagnostique et thérapeutique majeur, en particulier chez l’enfant, plus exposé aux formes graves [3]. À l’échelle mondiale, environ 390 millions de cas de dengue surviennent chaque année et 3,9 milliards de personnes réparties dans 128 pays sont exposées au risque d’infection [4]. En 2022, le Burkina Faso a notifié 11 656 675 cas de paludisme, dont 539 488 formes graves et 4 243 décès, parmi lesquels 2 925 enfants de moins de 5 ans [5]. Des données récentes issues de la région du Guiriko (Burkina Faso) rapportent une prévalence de la coïnfection paludisme-dengue variant de 7,1 % (coïnfection aiguë confirmée par RT-PCR) à 17,6 % (exposition dengue récente ou passée associée au paludisme), avec une recrudescence en fin de saison des pluies [6]. En Afrique, la prévalence de la coïnfection Plasmodium falciparum-dengue a significativement augmenté, passant de 0,9 % sur la période 2008-2013 à 5,5 % sur la période 2018-2021 [7]. Au Cameroun, un taux de coïnfection de 19,5 % a été rapporté chez l’enfant fébrile [8]. Au Burkina Faso, des taux respectifs de 12,9 % et 20,4 % ont été retrouvés par Yankéné [9] et par Ly [10]. Toutefois, les données pédiatriques concernant cette coïnfection demeurent rares dans notre pays. L’objectif de cette étude était de décrire les aspects épidémiologiques, cliniques, thérapeutiques et évolutifs de la coïnfection paludisme-dengue chez les enfants de moins de 15 ans pris en charge au CHU de Bogodogo (Ouagadougou) du 1er janvier au 31 décembre 2024, afin de contribuer à l’amélioration de leur prise en charge. 2. Patients et méthode L’étude s’est déroulée dans le service de pédiatrie médicale du Centre Hospitalier Universitaire de Bogodogo (CHU-B), structure de troisième niveau de référence à Ouagadougou, comportant une unité des urgences pédiatriques, une unité d’hospitalisation d’une capacité de 30 lits et une unité de néonatologie. Il s’agissait d’une étude transversale, à collecte de données rétrospective, à visée descriptive, portant sur la période du 1er janvier au 31 décembre 2024. Tous les enfants de moins de 15 ans ayant présenté simultanément un paludisme et une dengue au cours de leur prise en charge dans le service durant la période d’étude ont été inclus de façon exhaustive. Étaient exclus les dossiers inexploitables, c’est-à-dire sans informations cliniques suffisantes, sans diagnostic précis ou sans évolution clinique précisée. Les données sociodémographiques, anthropométriques, cliniques, paracliniques, thérapeutiques et évolutives ont été recueillies à partir des dossiers médicaux à l’aide d’une fiche de collecte standardisée et anonyme, l’enquêteur n’utilisant que le numéro de dossier. Le paludisme grave était défini selon les critères de l’Organisation mondiale de la santé, et la dengue classée en dengue probable sans signe d’alerte, dengue probable avec signe(s) d’alerte, ou dengue sévère, conformément aux directives nationales de prise en charge de la dengue au Burkina Faso [1]. (ahead of print) www.reducritic.com Fecha de recepción: 18-02-2025 Fecha de aceptación: 23-03-2025 DOI: 10.24875/RECC.25000003 Revista de Educación en Cuidados Críticos Resumen El dengue es la zoonosis más prevalente del mundo. En Latinoamérica, el número básico de reproducción aumentó un 54% en los últimos 60 años. La aparición de miocarditis clasifica al dengue como grave. Dicha complicación tiene una prevalen­ cia del 11% en los casos graves y una mortalidad de hasta el 38%. A continuación, se presenta el caso de una adulta mayor, hipertensa, dislipidémica, diabética y con osteopenia, que después de la fase febril del dengue inició con insuficien­ cia cardiaca aguda. Se trató con vasopresores, inotrópicos, esteroides y balón de contrapulsación aórtica. La paciente logró resolver el shock cardiogénico y recuperar por completo la función sistólica y diastólica del ventrículo izquierdo. Palabras clave: Dengue. Dengue grave. Choque cardiogénico. Miocarditis. Abstract Dengue is the most prevalent zoonosis in the world. In Latin America, the basic reproduction number has increased by 54% in the last 60 years. The appearance of myocarditis classifies dengue as severe. This complication has a prevalence of 11% in severe cases and a mortality rate of up to 38%. We present the case of an elderly woman with hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes and osteopenia who, after the febrile phase of dengue, began an acute heart failure. She was treated with vaso­ pressors, inotropes, steroids and an intra-aortic balloon pump. The patient resolved cardiogenic shock and fully recovered left ventricular systolic and diastolic function. Keywords: Dengue. Severe dengue. Cardiogenic shock. Myocarditis. 2 REduCRítiC. (ahead of print) Introducción El dengue es la zoonosis más prevalente en el mundo. Ocurren 390 millones de infecciones anuales, de las cuales 96 millones tienen manifestaciones clínicas. De los casos totales de dengue solo el 0.16% desarrolla dengue grave. De los casos graves que requieren hos- pitalización, el 10% muere por la enfermedad1-4. Hasta el 24 de octubre del 2024 el Ministerio de Salud de Costa Rica había reportado 22,575 casos de dengue y seis fallecidos directamente por la enferme- dad. En comparación, en el 2023 hubo 10,236 casos (aumentó más del doble) y desde el 2013 no se repor- taban fallecimientos por dicha enfermedad5,6. Según el reporte Lancet Countdown Latinoamérica 2023, el número básico de reproducción (capacidad de un individuo infectado de causar casos secundarios) del dengue aumentó un 54% en los últimos 60 años y eso es debido a que el mosquito ahora es capaz de sobre- vivir en zonas en las que antes no podía, debido al aumento de la temperatura7. Las condiciones ambientales actuales y los datos que se tienen hasta ahora parecen indicar que los casos van a continuar aumentando año a año y por lo tanto también los casos graves y las complicaciones poco frecuentes por la enfermedad. A continuación se presenta el caso de un choque cardiogénico por dengue (segunda infección). Caso clínico Se trata de una paciente de 62 años, conocida con hipertensión arterial, dislipidemia, diabetes mellitus tipo 2 y osteopenia, con antecedente de síndrome febril agudo, autolimitado hace siete años, que según afirma la familia se trató de dengue. Consultó al servicio de emergencias con historia de siete días de evolución de malestar general, sensación febril, dolor torácico intermitente, no asociado a esfuer- zos y el nexo epidemiológico de que a varias de las personas que viven con ella se les diagnosticó dengue recientemente. En la valoración inicial se documentó taquicardia, hipo- tensión, llenado capilar lento, diaforesis, elevación difusa del ST y por ecocardiograma transtorácico (ECOTT) derrame pericárdico moderado, hipocinesia difusa mode- rada y trastornos segmentarios en reposo; además de troponina T positivas y en ascenso (inicial en 91.8 ng/l y la segunda en 237 ng/l). Debido a choque cardiogénico se iniciaron vasopre- sores e inotrópicos y ante la sospecha de infarto agudo de miocardio con elevación del ST, se realizó catete­ rismo coronario, que resultó con arterias coronarias sin lesiones angiográficamente significativas. Ante la sospecha de miocarditis, se decidió iniciar metilprednisolona intravenosa 125 mg IV al día. A pesar de vasopresores e inotrópicos, en las siguien­ tes 24 h la paciente continuó empeorando, por lo que se colocó un balón de contrapulsación intraaórtico y se administró levosimendán. Con lo anterior logró resolver el shock cardiogénico y los cambios en el ECOTT inicial revirtieron por completo. Por la sospecha de miocarditis viral, durante su estancia en la unidad se tomaron pruebas moleculares por virus tropicales y respiratorios y serologías virales. Todas resultaron negativas, excepto la prueba de reac­ ción en cadena de la polimerasa por dengue (umbral de ciclos: 38) y la inmunoglobulina (Ig)M por dengue (no se logró documentar seroconversión a IgG durante el internamiento). Ante los hallazgos anteriores, se cata­ logó como dengue grave, por la miocarditis. Durante la estancia hospitalaria, como complicacio­ nes tuvo hipernatremia hiperclorémica, hiperglucemia, encefalopatía y plaquetopenia (comenzó en el segundo día de internamiento y se mantuvo por 15 días). No tuvo sangrados. Discusión El dengue es un flavivirus, ARN de cadena simple, de la familia flaviviridae. Existen cinco serotipos de dengue, pero solo cuatro afectan a los humanos (DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3 y DENV-4). Los vectores son los mosquitos urbanos Aedes aegypti y Aedes albopictus, que son endémicos de regiones tropicales y subtropicales. Cuando el mos­ quito pica al humano, inocula el virus en la piel, donde infecta a macrófagos, células dendríticas y células de Langerhans, que migran a nódulos linfáticos, donde infectan otras células y provocan la viremia. El virus termina infectando células endoteliales, células madre, células del estroma hematopoyético, megacariocitos, plaquetas, neuronas y miocitos cardiacos1,2,8,9. Después de la primera infección se forma inmunidad a largo plazo contra el serotipo responsable (inmunidad homotípica) y durante un periodo corto contra otros serotipos (inmunidad heterotípica). Luego quedan cir­ culando anticuerpos homotípicos neutralizantes y anti­ cuerpos heterotípicos no neutralizantes. En una segunda infección, por un serotipo diferente, los anticuerpos hete­ rotípicos no neutralizantes persistentes se unen a los antí­ genos del serotipo nuevo y forman complejos que facilitan L. Saborío-Morales, L.B. Montero-Chacón. Choque cardiogénico por dengue 3 la entrada del virus a las células, lo que hace la infección más grave. La reacción cruzada leve entre las células T previamente activadas y el nuevo serotipo induce la pro­ ducción de citocinas proinflamatorias, que puede resultar en una tormenta de citocinas. A este fenómeno se le llama inmunopotenciación mediada por anticuerpos1,2. La presencia de miocarditis, como en este caso, clasi­ fica al dengue en grave. A pesar de que no suele ser la presentación más común, hay estudios que indican pre­ valencias hasta del 11% y mortalidad de hasta el 38%10,11. Lo descrito hasta ahora (en reportes de casos) con respecto al tratamiento es dar medidas de soporte8,12, incluso se ha descrito hasta el uso de oxigenación por membrana extracorpórea veno-arterial (ECMO V-A)13. No existen estudios que indiquen que el uso de este­ roides sea útil, aunque existe un reporte de caso de mejoría drástica con una sola dosis de metilpredniso­ lona14 y en reportes de población pediátrica se ha rela­ cionado el uso de esteroides con el aumento en la fracción de eyección15. La Organización Mundial de la Salud recomienda no utilizar esteroides en pacientes con dengue grave16. Conclusión En países tropicales, como Costa Rica, el dengue es cada vez más prevalente y no parece que dicha tenden­ cia vaya a disminuir. Lo anterior hace más frecuente la aparición de cuadros graves y complicaciones raras, como la miocarditis, que posee una alta mortalidad. Por lo tanto, es relevante poder identificar dicho cuadro clí­ nico, para poder tratarlo de forma temprana y eficaz. Consideraciones éticas Protección de personas y animales. Los autores declaran que para esta investigación no se han reali­ zado experimentos en seres humanos ni en animales. Confidencialidad de los datos. Los autores decla­ ran que han seguido los protocolos de su centro de trabajo sobre la publicación de datos de pacientes. Derecho a la privacidad y consentimiento informado. Los autores han obtenido el consentimiento informado de los pacientes y/o sujetos referidos en el artículo. Montero-Chacón Unidad de Cuidados Intensivos Médicos, Hospital México, San José, Costa Rica CASO CLÍNICO *Correspondencia: Lachiner Saborío-Morales E-mail: lachiner7@gmail.com 2938-1304 / © 2025 Asociación Salvadoreña de Medicina Crítica y Cuidados Intensivos (ASALMECCI). Publicado por Permanyer. Éste es un artículo open access bajo la licencia CC BY‐NC‐ND (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/). Disponible en internet: 05-05-2025 REduCrític. (ahead of print) www.reducritic.com Fecha de recepción: 18-02-2025 Fecha de aceptación: 23-03-2025 DOI: 10.24875/RECC.25000003 Revista de Educación en Cuidados Críticos Resumen El dengue es la zoonosis más prevalente del mundo. En Latinoamérica, el número básico de reproducción aumentó un 54% en los últimos 60 años. La aparición de miocarditis clasifica al dengue como grave. Dicha complicación tiene una prevalen­ cia del 11% en los casos graves y una mortalidad de hasta el 38%. A continuación, se presenta el caso de una adulta mayor, hipertensa, dislipidémica, diabética y con osteopenia, que después de la fase febril del dengue inició con insuficien­ cia cardiaca aguda. Se trató con vasopresores, inotrópicos, esteroides y balón de contrapulsación aórtica. La paciente logró resolver el shock cardiogénico y recuperar por completo la función sistólica y diastólica del ventrículo izquierdo. Palabras clave: Dengue. Dengue grave. Choque cardiogénico. Miocarditis. Abstract Dengue is the most prevalent zoonosis in the world. In Latin America, the basic reproduction number has increased by 54% in the last 60 years. The appearance of myocarditis classifies dengue as severe. This complication has a prevalence of 11% in severe cases and a mortality rate of up to 38%. We present the case of an elderly woman with hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes and osteopenia who, after the febrile phase of dengue, began an acute heart failure. She was treated with vaso­ pressors, inotropes, steroids and an intra-aortic balloon pump. The patient resolved cardiogenic shock and fully recovered left ventricular systolic and diastolic function. Keywords: Dengue. Severe dengue. Cardiogenic shock. Myocarditis. 2 REduCRítiC. (ahead of print) Introducción El dengue es la zoonosis más prevalente en el mundo. Ocurren 390 millones de infecciones anuales, de las cuales 96 millones tienen manifestaciones clínicas. De los casos totales de dengue solo el 0.16% desarrolla dengue grave. De los casos graves que requieren hos- pitalización, el 10% muere por la enfermedad1-4. Hasta el 24 de octubre del 2024 el Ministerio de Salud de Costa Rica había reportado 22,575 casos de dengue y seis fallecidos directamente por la enferme- dad. En comparación, en el 2023 hubo 10,236 casos (aumentó más del doble) y desde el 2013 no se repor- taban fallecimientos por dicha enfermedad5,6. Según el reporte Lancet Countdown Latinoamérica 2023, el número básico de reproducción (capacidad de un individuo infectado de causar casos secundarios) del dengue aumentó un 54% en los últimos 60 años y eso es debido a que el mosquito ahora es capaz de sobre- vivir en zonas en las que antes no podía, debido al aumento de la temperatura7. Las condiciones ambientales actuales y los datos que se tienen hasta ahora parecen indicar que los casos van a continuar aumentando año a año y por lo tanto también los casos graves y las complicaciones poco frecuentes por la enfermedad. A continuación se presenta el caso de un choque cardiogénico por dengue (segunda infección). Caso clínico Se trata de una paciente de 62 años, conocida con hipertensión arterial, dislipidemia, diabetes mellitus tipo 2 y osteopenia, con antecedente de síndrome febril agudo, autolimitado hace siete años, que según afirma la familia se trató de dengue. Consultó al servicio de emergencias con historia de siete días de evolución de malestar general, sensación febril, dolor torácico intermitente, no asociado a esfuer- zos y el nexo epidemiológico de que a varias de las personas que viven con ella se les diagnosticó dengue recientemente. En la valoración inicial se documentó taquicardia, hipo- tensión, llenado capilar lento, diaforesis, elevación difusa del ST y por ecocardiograma transtorácico (ECOTT) derrame pericárdico moderado, hipocinesia difusa mode- rada y trastornos segmentarios en reposo; además de troponina T positivas y en ascenso (inicial en 91.8 ng/l y la segunda en 237 ng/l). Debido a choque cardiogénico se iniciaron vasopre- sores e inotrópicos y ante la sospecha de infarto agudo de miocardio con elevación del ST, se realizó catete­ rismo coronario, que resultó con arterias coronarias sin lesiones angiográficamente significativas. Ante la sospecha de miocarditis, se decidió iniciar metilprednisolona intravenosa 125 mg IV al día. A pesar de vasopresores e inotrópicos, en las siguien­ tes 24 h la paciente continuó empeorando, por lo que se colocó un balón de contrapulsación intraaórtico y se administró levosimendán. Con lo anterior logró resolver el shock cardiogénico y los cambios en el ECOTT inicial revirtieron por completo. Por la sospecha de miocarditis viral, durante su estancia en la unidad se tomaron pruebas moleculares por virus tropicales y respiratorios y serologías virales. Todas resultaron negativas, excepto la prueba de reac­ ción en cadena de la polimerasa por dengue (umbral de ciclos: 38) y la inmunoglobulina (Ig)M por dengue (no se logró documentar seroconversión a IgG durante el internamiento). Ante los hallazgos anteriores, se cata­ logó como dengue grave, por la miocarditis. Durante la estancia hospitalaria, como complicacio­ nes tuvo hipernatremia hiperclorémica, hiperglucemia, encefalopatía y plaquetopenia (comenzó en el segundo día de internamiento y se mantuvo por 15 días). No tuvo sangrados. Discusión El dengue es un flavivirus, ARN de cadena simple, de la familia flaviviridae. Existen cinco serotipos de dengue, pero solo cuatro afectan a los humanos (DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3 y DENV-4). Los vectores son los mosquitos urbanos Aedes aegypti y Aedes albopictus, que son endémicos de regiones tropicales y subtropicales. Cuando el mos­ quito pica al humano, inocula el virus en la piel, donde infecta a macrófagos, células dendríticas y células de Langerhans, que migran a nódulos linfáticos, donde infectan otras células y provocan la viremia. El virus termina infectando células endoteliales, células madre, células del estroma hematopoyético, megacariocitos, plaquetas, neuronas y miocitos cardiacos1,2,8,9. Después de la primera infección se forma inmunidad a largo plazo contra el serotipo responsable (inmunidad homotípica) y durante un periodo corto contra otros serotipos (inmunidad heterotípica). Luego quedan cir­ culando anticuerpos homotípicos neutralizantes y anti­ cuerpos heterotípicos no neutralizantes. En una segunda infección, por un serotipo diferente, los anticuerpos hete­ rotípicos no neutralizantes persistentes se unen a los antí­ genos del serotipo nuevo y forman complejos que facilitan L. La reacción cruzada leve entre las células T previamente activadas y el nuevo serotipo induce la pro­ ducción de citocinas proinflamatorias, que puede resultar en una tormenta de citocinas. full_text: AbstractTick-borne encephalitis virus (TBEV) invades the central nervous system (CNS) through strain-specific mechanisms that remain poorly understood. For mosquito-borne orthoflaviviruses such as dengue and yellow fever viruses, the nonstructural protein 1 (NS1) has been shown to disrupt endothelial barrier integrity by targeting tight junction proteins (TJPs), facilitating viral neuroinvasion. However, comparable mechanisms in TBEVs remain largely unexplored. Here, we investigated the potential interaction of NS1 from high (Hypr)- and low (Vs)-pathogenic TBEV strains with different blood–brain barrier (BBB) TJPs, using AlphaFold3 (AF3) multimer modeling and in vitro binding assays. AF3 modeling suggested that NS1 from the highly pathogenic strain may interact with multiple TJPs, including junctional adhesion molecule A (JAM-A), a key component of the paracellular barrier. In contrast, the low-pathogenic Vs showed a more restricted interaction profile. Experimental validation using recombinant NS1 proteins revealed strain-specific binding profiles: Hypr NS1 displayed high-affinity, saturable direct binding to immobilized JAM-A (KD,app = 0.81 nM), whereas Vs NS1 showed no binding. Immunofluorescence assays on human lung epithelial (A549) and BBB (hCMEC/D3) cells further demonstrated colocalization between Hypr NS1 and JAM-A, supporting a potential interaction. No direct binding to ZO-1, a barrier scaffold lacking an extracellular domain, was observed for either strain. This differential interaction profile may be modulated by 22 amino acids localized to the Wing and β-Ladder domains within NS1, which distinguish Hypr from Vs. Notably, despite its limited interactions with the investigated TJPs, the Vs strain is associated with slow-progressive infections that can culminate in chronic neurological disease. This highlights the need for further studies into noncanonical pathways of neuroinvasion. MethodsRecombinant TBEV NS Protein Generation and PurificationN-terminally His-tagged Vs (accession number: AF069066.1) or Hypr (accession number: U39292.1) NS1 was heterologously expressed in E. coli BL21 Gold cells harboring the pET-28a-TEV-NS1 plasmid (synthesized by GenScript). Protein was expressed in LB medium containing 50 μg/mL kanamycin. Briefly, cultures were incubated at 37 °C, with shaking at 200 rpm until an OD600 nm of ∼0.6 was reached. Protein expression was induced with 1 mM IPTG and cultures were incubated at 25 °C overnight with shaking at 200 rpm. Cells were harvested by centrifugation at 4500 × g for 30 min at 4 °C. Cell pellets were resuspended in 50 mM Tris-HCl, 500 mM NaCl, 2 mM MgCl2, 10 mM imidazole, 10% v/v glycerol, pH 8.0, containing Benzonase (Merck) and cOmplete EDTA-free protease inhibitors (Roche), and lysed by sonication on ice prior to centrifugation at 11,000 × g at 4 °C for 20 min. NS1 was located in the insoluble fraction and recovered via on-column refolding. The insoluble fraction was resuspended in denaturing buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl, 300 mM NaCl, 20 mM imidazole, 5 M guanidine HCl, 10 mM DTT, pH 8.0) and incubated on ice for 1 h before centrifugation at 13,000 × g for 20 min at 4 °C. Extracted proteins were added to a Ni-NTA column (Qiagen) and washed with denaturing buffer. A gradient wash was performed, gradually reducing the guanidine HCl and DTT concentrations to 0 M. The column was further washed in refolding buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl, 300 mM NaCl, 20 mM imidazole, pH 8.0). Protein was eluted in buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl, 300 mM NaCl, 500 mM imidazole, pH 8.0) and purity was assessed using SDS-PAGE. Purified NS1 was exchanged into 50 mM Tris-HCl, 500 mM NaCl, 2 mM MgCl2, 10 mM imidazole, 10% v/v glycerol, pH 8.0, and stored at −80 °C.Circular Dichroism (CD)Successful refolding was assessed using CD spectroscopy as described previously , and compared to commercially available NS1. Briefly, CD measurements were performed using a JASCO (model J-715) spectropolarimeter. Spectra were recorded in 0.1 cm path-length quartz cells at a protein concentration of 2 μM in 10 mM phosphate buffer at pH 8.0. Three consecutive scans were compiled (180–260 nM) and average spectra were stored. Observed raw ellipticities were converted to molar ellipticity (θ). Secondary structures were estimated from fitted far-UV spectra using the DichroWeb server (http://dichroweb.cryst.bbk.ac.uk/html/home.shtml).Multiple Sequence Alignment and Percent Identity Matrix GenerationNS1 protein sequences of TBEV isolates and closely related tick-borne orthoflaviviruses were downloaded from the NCBI (Vasilchenko [accession number; AF069066.1], Hypr [U39292.1], Neudoerfl [U27495.1], Zausaev [AF527415.1], UK-Thetford-Forest [MN128700.1], UK-Hampshire-2019 [MN661145.1], Sofjin-Ru [JN229223.1], Mandal-2009 [KF991107.1], NL [LC171402], Baikalian [EF469661.1], Himalaya-1 [MG599476.1], and other closely related TBFV (Louping-ill-virus [Y07863.1], Langat-virus_[NC_003690.1] and Powassan virus [NC_003687.1]) and aligned using ClustalW, as implemented in BioEdit (Figure ).2Sequence alignment of NS1 proteins from tick-borne orthoflaviviruses (TBFV). NS1 proteins of different TBFVs were compared using a multiple alignment tool, CLUSTAL Omega. This showed conserved regions among the NS1 sequences, indicated as percentage (%) sequence identity from highlighted areas of similarity (100%; dark purple) to dissimilarity (0; white). The consensus for all 14 sequences is indicated at the top. Alignments are grouped into TBEV isolates (Vasilchenko [accession number; AF069066.1], Hypr [U39292.1], Neudoerfl [U27495.1], Zausaev [AF527415.1], UK-Thetford-Forest [MN128700.1], UK-Hampshire-2019 [MN661145.1], Sofjin-Ru [JN229223.1], Mandal-2009 [KF991107.1], NL [LC171402], Baikalian [EF469661.1], Himalaya-1­[MG599476.1], and other closely related TBFVs (Louping-ill-virus [Y07863.1], Langat-virus_[NC_003690.1], and Powassan [NC_003687.1]. Sequence conservation of total alignments with less than 20% of gaps and BLOSUM62 alignment quality are shown.Default parameters were used unless otherwise specified, including the Gonnet substitution matrix, a gap-opening penalty of 10, and a gap-extension penalty of 0.2. Following alignment, a percent identity matrix (PIM) was generated, which calculates the pairwise percentage of identical residues between aligned sequences. This matrix provided a quantitative measure of sequence similarity and was used to assess evolutionary relationships and sequence conservation.NS1–BBB TJP Interaction Predictions and Interface Analysis by AlphaFold3 (AF3)Predicted interactions between TBEV Hypr or Vs NS1 and host TJPs were modeled using AF3. , AF3 structural predictions were visualized using PyMOL (https://pymol.org/2/). Briefly, the NS1–TJP complex was loaded into PyMOL, and residues at the protein–protein interface were selected manually based on proximity and surface contact. The “find polar contacts” function was used to detect potential hydrogen bonds and salt bridges between the proteins. Interacting residue pairs were further refined by selecting only those forming direct contacts between NS1 and TJP.Distances between interacting atoms were measured using the “distance” measurement tool in PyMOL. All interacting residue pairs were ranked based on the shortest interatomic distance. Top-ranking interactions (those with the shortest and most structurally significant contacts) were visualized and annotated in the PyMOL structural model. A complete list of all detected interactions, including residue identities and distances, is shown in Supplementary Tables S3–S5.Molecular Docking and Thermodynamic AnalysisNS1–TJP docking was performed using the HDOCK web server (http://hdock.phys.hust.edu.cn/), which uses a hybrid scoring function combining template-based modeling and free docking algorithms. Homodimers of NS1 proteins from TBEV Hypr and Vs strains were docked against several human full-length proteins or extracellular domains, including Claudin-5, Claudin-10, JAM-A, JAM-B, and JAM-C. Docking scores were recorded as a proxy for binding energy, with higher negative scores indicating stronger predicted interactions. Docking was performed in the default mode, allowing the server to automatically identify potential binding sites and generate a ranked list of predicted complex models.To estimate binding affinities under physiological (25 °C, 298.15 K) and febrile (40 °C, 313.15 K) conditions, Gibbs free energy (ΔG) and equilibrium dissociation constants (KD) were calculated from docking scores using the thermodynamic equation:ΔG=−RTlnKD⇒KD=e−ΔG/RTwhere R is the gas constant (0.001987 kcal·mol–1·K–1) and T is the temperature in Kelvin. We assumed docking scores approximate ΔG in kcal/mol, consistent with prior benchmarks for HDOCK scoring. , Fold changes in KD between 25 °C and 40 °C were computed to assess temperature sensitivity (Supplementary Table S1).Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA) for NS1–JAM-A/ZO-1 InteractionHigh-binding 96-well plates were coated with recombinant human JAM-A (Kactus, HM10A) or ZO-1 (Invitrogen, RP-99371) at a concentration of 1 μg/mL in 0.1 M sodium bicarbonate buffer (pH 9.6) and incubated for 2 h at room temperature (RT). Wells were washed three times with PBS containing 0.1% Tween-20 (PBS-T), followed by blocking with 5% bovine serum albumin (BSA) in PBS supplemented with 0.1 mM EDTA for 1 h at RT. Recombinant NS1 proteins from TBEV Hypr or Vs strains (variable starting concentrations as indicated: 0.5, 1, or 2 μg/mL) were 2-fold serially diluted and incubated for 2 h at RT. For comparison, Hypr NS1 produced in mammalian HEK293 cells (Native Antigen; starting concentrations 0.25, 0.5, 1, or 2 μg/mL) was analyzed under the same experimental format (96-well) and conditions to assess NS1–JAM-A binding. After washing (3× with PBS-T), bound NS1 was detected using mouse anti-TBEV NS1 monoclonal antibodies (R&D Systems, MAB10106; 0.05 μg/mL), followed by incubation with HRP-conjugated anti-mouse IgG (Sigma, A9044; 1:40,000) for 1 h at RT. Plates were washed and incubated with TMB peroxidase substrate (Sigma, T5569) in the dark for up to 30 min at RT. The reaction was stopped with 1 M hydrochloric acid. Absorbance was measured at 450 nm using a NanoQuant Infinite M200 plate reader (Tecan).Raw OD450 values from technical replicates were averaged and analyzed using Python (SciPy, NumPy, and Matplotlib). NS1 concentrations were converted from mass concentrations (μg mL–1) to molar concentrations (M) with a molecular mass of 48 kDa for recombinant NS1. Apparent equilibrium dissociation constants (KD,app) were estimated by nonlinear least-squares regression on the untransformed molar concentrations using a one-site specific binding model:Y=(Bmax×[NS1])/(KD,app+[NS1])where Y is the measured OD450, Bmax is the maximum binding response, [NS1] is the untransformed molar concentration, and KD,app is the apparent equilibrium dissociation constant. Nonlinear regression was performed using the SciPy curve_fit function. Concentration–response curves were displayed on a log10 (molar concentration) axis for graphical presentation only; logarithmic transformations were not used for parameter estimation. For ZO-1 experiments, concentration–response data showed no saturable binding suitable for equilibrium binding analysis. Consequently, KD,app values were not determined. Data are presented as mean ± SD with descriptive trend lines.For statistical analysis, OD450 values obtained at selected NS1 concentrations (0.25 μg/mL and 1 μg/mL) were compared between Hypr and Vs NS1 using an unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-test. Statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05.Plots were generated using Matplotlib in Python. Concentration–response curves are presented as the mean ± SD with the corresponding nonlinear regression fit (JAM-A) or descriptive trend lines (ZO-1). Bar graphs show the mean ± SD for the indicated NS1 concentrations.Immunofluorescence (IF) Analysis of Replicon-Transfected CellsHypr and Vs replicon systems have been described elsewhere. Briefly, structural genes (nts 183-2386) were removed to make them noninfectious. To ensure correct polyprotein processing and NS1 translocation to the ER, a ribosome-stuttering 2A peptide from foot-and-mouth disease virus (FMDV) was incorporated downstream of the luc-cu sequence prior to the transmembrane (TM) region of E (22 codons). Cells were washed in PBS and stained with 1:500 fluorochrome-conjugated secondary antibodies (Thermo Fisher) in PBS-T containing 1% wt/vol BSA for 1 h at RT in the dark. Confocal microscopy images were acquired on a Zeiss LSM880 microscope with a Airyscan or an Olympus FV3000. Postacquisition analysis was performed using Zen software (Zen version 2015 black edition 2.3, Zeiss) or Fiji (v1.49) software. Image AnalysisImages were analyzed using the Fiji package for ImageJ. For colocalization analyses, Manders’ overlap coefficients were calculated using Fiji software with the Just Another Co-localization Plugin (JACoP) (National Institutes of Health), , where the M1 coefficient reports the fraction of the NS1 signal that overlaps with the JAM-A signal, whilst the M2 coefficient reports the fraction of the JAM-A signal overlapping with the NS1 signal. Inserts were equilibrated for 10 min at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO2 prior to assessment. TEER values were normalized to the surface area of the Transwell membrane and expressed as Ω·cm2. Where applicable, a two-way ANOVA was used to assess interactions between strain and concentration, with a Bonferroni correction applied for multiple testing. Thresholds for statistical significance were set at: p < 0.05 (*), p < 0.01 (**), p < 0.001 (***), p < 0.0001 (****). All data are presented as the mean ± SEM unless otherwise stated. full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractTick-borne encephalitis virus (TBEV) invades the central nervous system (CNS) through strain-specific mechanisms that remain poorly understood. For mosquito-borne orthoflaviviruses such as dengue and yellow fever viruses, the nonstructural protein 1 (NS1) has been shown to disrupt endothelial barrier integrity by targeting tight junction proteins (TJPs), facilitating viral neuroinvasion. However, comparable mechanisms in TBEVs remain largely unexplored. Here, we investigated the potential interaction of NS1 from high (Hypr)- and low (Vs)-pathogenic TBEV strains with different blood–brain barrier (BBB) TJPs, using AlphaFold3 (AF3) multimer modeling and in vitro binding assays. AF3 modeling suggested that NS1 from the highly pathogenic strain may interact with multiple TJPs, including junctional adhesion molecule A (JAM-A), a key component of the paracellular barrier. In contrast, the low-pathogenic Vs showed a more restricted interaction profile. Experimental validation using recombinant NS1 proteins revealed strain-specific binding profiles: Hypr NS1 displayed high-affinity, saturable direct binding to immobilized JAM-A (KD,app = 0.81 nM), whereas Vs NS1 showed no binding. Immunofluorescence assays on human lung epithelial (A549) and BBB (hCMEC/D3) cells further demonstrated colocalization between Hypr NS1 and JAM-A, supporting a potential interaction. No direct binding to ZO-1, a barrier scaffold lacking an extracellular domain, was observed for either strain. This differential interaction profile may be modulated by 22 amino acids localized to the Wing and β-Ladder domains within NS1, which distinguish Hypr from Vs. Notably, despite its limited interactions with the investigated TJPs, the Vs strain is associated with slow-progressive infections that can culminate in chronic neurological disease. This highlights the need for further studies into noncanonical pathways of neuroinvasion.
full_text_sections.methods: MethodsRecombinant TBEV NS Protein Generation and PurificationN-terminally His-tagged Vs (accession number: AF069066.1) or Hypr (accession number: U39292.1) NS1 was heterologously expressed in E. coli BL21 Gold cells harboring the pET-28a-TEV-NS1 plasmid (synthesized by GenScript). Protein was expressed in LB medium containing 50 μg/mL kanamycin. Briefly, cultures were incubated at 37 °C, with shaking at 200 rpm until an OD600 nm of ∼0.6 was reached. Protein expression was induced with 1 mM IPTG and cultures were incubated at 25 °C overnight with shaking at 200 rpm. Cells were harvested by centrifugation at 4500 × g for 30 min at 4 °C. Cell pellets were resuspended in 50 mM Tris-HCl, 500 mM NaCl, 2 mM MgCl2, 10 mM imidazole, 10% v/v glycerol, pH 8.0, containing Benzonase (Merck) and cOmplete EDTA-free protease inhibitors (Roche), and lysed by sonication on ice prior to centrifugation at 11,000 × g at 4 °C for 20 min. NS1 was located in the insoluble fraction and recovered via on-column refolding. The insoluble fraction was resuspended in denaturing buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl, 300 mM NaCl, 20 mM imidazole, 5 M guanidine HCl, 10 mM DTT, pH 8.0) and incubated on ice for 1 h before centrifugation at 13,000 × g for 20 min at 4 °C. Extracted proteins were added to a Ni-NTA column (Qiagen) and washed with denaturing buffer. A gradient wash was performed, gradually reducing the guanidine HCl and DTT concentrations to 0 M. The column was further washed in refolding buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl, 300 mM NaCl, 20 mM imidazole, pH 8.0). Protein was eluted in buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl, 300 mM NaCl, 500 mM imidazole, pH 8.0) and purity was assessed using SDS-PAGE. Purified NS1 was exchanged into 50 mM Tris-HCl, 500 mM NaCl, 2 mM MgCl2, 10 mM imidazole, 10% v/v glycerol, pH 8.0, and stored at −80 °C.Circular Dichroism (CD)Successful refolding was assessed using CD spectroscopy as described previously , and compared to commercially available NS1. Briefly, CD measurements were performed using a JASCO (model J-715) spectropolarimeter. Spectra were recorded in 0.1 cm path-length quartz cells at a protein concentration of 2 μM in 10 mM phosphate buffer at pH 8.0. Three consecutive scans were compiled (180–260 nM) and average spectra were stored. Observed raw ellipticities were converted to molar ellipticity (θ). Secondary structures were estimated from fitted far-UV spectra using the DichroWeb server (http://dichroweb.cryst.bbk.ac.uk/html/home.shtml).Multiple Sequence Alignment and Percent Identity Matrix GenerationNS1 protein sequences of TBEV isolates and closely related tick-borne orthoflaviviruses were downloaded from the NCBI (Vasilchenko [accession number; AF069066.1], Hypr [U39292.1], Neudoerfl [U27495.1], Zausaev [AF527415.1], UK-Thetford-Forest [MN128700.1], UK-Hampshire-2019 [MN661145.1], Sofjin-Ru [JN229223.1], Mandal-2009 [KF991107.1], NL [LC171402], Baikalian [EF469661.1], Himalaya-1 [MG599476.1], and other closely related TBFV (Louping-ill-virus [Y07863.1], Langat-virus_[NC_003690.1] and Powassan virus [NC_003687.1]) and aligned using ClustalW, as implemented in BioEdit (Figure ).2Sequence alignment of NS1 proteins from tick-borne orthoflaviviruses (TBFV). NS1 proteins of different TBFVs were compared using a multiple alignment tool, CLUSTAL Omega. This showed conserved regions among the NS1 sequences, indicated as percentage (%) sequence identity from highlighted areas of similarity (100%; dark purple) to dissimilarity (0; white). The consensus for all 14 sequences is indicated at the top. Alignments are grouped into TBEV isolates (Vasilchenko [accession number; AF069066.1], Hypr [U39292.1], Neudoerfl [U27495.1], Zausaev [AF527415.1], UK-Thetford-Forest [MN128700.1], UK-Hampshire-2019 [MN661145.1], Sofjin-Ru [JN229223.1], Mandal-2009 [KF991107.1], NL [LC171402], Baikalian [EF469661.1], Himalaya-1­[MG599476.1], and other closely related TBFVs (Louping-ill-virus [Y07863.1], Langat-virus_[NC_003690.1], and Powassan [NC_003687.1]. Sequence conservation of total alignments with less than 20% of gaps and BLOSUM62 alignment quality are shown.Default parameters were used unless otherwise specified, including the Gonnet substitution matrix, a gap-opening penalty of 10, and a gap-extension penalty of 0.2. Following alignment, a percent identity matrix (PIM) was generated, which calculates the pairwise percentage of identical residues between aligned sequences. This matrix provided a quantitative measure of sequence similarity and was used to assess evolutionary relationships and sequence conservation.NS1–BBB TJP Interaction Predictions and Interface Analysis by AlphaFold3 (AF3)Predicted interactions between TBEV Hypr or Vs NS1 and host TJPs were modeled using AF3. , AF3 structural predictions were visualized using PyMOL (https://pymol.org/2/). Briefly, the NS1–TJP complex was loaded into PyMOL, and residues at the protein–protein interface were selected manually based on proximity and surface contact. The “find polar contacts” function was used to detect potential hydrogen bonds and salt bridges between the proteins. Interacting residue pairs were further refined by selecting only those forming direct contacts between NS1 and TJP.Distances between interacting atoms were measured using the “distance” measurement tool in PyMOL. All interacting residue pairs were ranked based on the shortest interatomic distance. Top-ranking interactions (those with the shortest and most structurally significant contacts) were visualized and annotated in the PyMOL structural model. A complete list of all detected interactions, including residue identities and distances, is shown in Supplementary Tables S3–S5.Molecular Docking and Thermodynamic AnalysisNS1–TJP docking was performed using the HDOCK web server (http://hdock.phys.hust.edu.cn/), which uses a hybrid scoring function combining template-based modeling and free docking algorithms. Homodimers of NS1 proteins from TBEV Hypr and Vs strains were docked against several human full-length proteins or extracellular domains, including Claudin-5, Claudin-10, JAM-A, JAM-B, and JAM-C. Docking scores were recorded as a proxy for binding energy, with higher negative scores indicating stronger predicted interactions. Docking was performed in the default mode, allowing the server to automatically identify potential binding sites and generate a ranked list of predicted complex models.To estimate binding affinities under physiological (25 °C, 298.15 K) and febrile (40 °C, 313.15 K) conditions, Gibbs free energy (ΔG) and equilibrium dissociation constants (KD) were calculated from docking scores using the thermodynamic equation:ΔG=−RTlnKD⇒KD=e−ΔG/RTwhere R is the gas constant (0.001987 kcal·mol–1·K–1) and T is the temperature in Kelvin. We assumed docking scores approximate ΔG in kcal/mol, consistent with prior benchmarks for HDOCK scoring. , Fold changes in KD between 25 °C and 40 °C were computed to assess temperature sensitivity (Supplementary Table S1).Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA) for NS1–JAM-A/ZO-1 InteractionHigh-binding 96-well plates were coated with recombinant human JAM-A (Kactus, HM10A) or ZO-1 (Invitrogen, RP-99371) at a concentration of 1 μg/mL in 0.1 M sodium bicarbonate buffer (pH 9.6) and incubated for 2 h at room temperature (RT). Wells were washed three times with PBS containing 0.1% Tween-20 (PBS-T), followed by blocking with 5% bovine serum albumin (BSA) in PBS supplemented with 0.1 mM EDTA for 1 h at RT. Recombinant NS1 proteins from TBEV Hypr or Vs strains (variable starting concentrations as indicated: 0.5, 1, or 2 μg/mL) were 2-fold serially diluted and incubated for 2 h at RT. For comparison, Hypr NS1 produced in mammalian HEK293 cells (Native Antigen; starting concentrations 0.25, 0.5, 1, or 2 μg/mL) was analyzed under the same experimental format (96-well) and conditions to assess NS1–JAM-A binding. After washing (3× with PBS-T), bound NS1 was detected using mouse anti-TBEV NS1 monoclonal antibodies (R&D Systems, MAB…
full_text_sections.results: ResultsRelative Diversity of NS1 Protein among Tick-Borne OrthoflavivirusesTo investigate the evolutionary relationships among tick-borne orthoflaviviruses (TBFVs), we generated pairwise percentage-identity matrices based on NS1 protein sequences from 14 viral isolates (Figure B). This panel included multiple TBEV strains, including recent isolates from the UK (Figure ) (Thetford-Forest [MN128700.1], Hampshire-2019 [MN661145.1]), and the Netherlands (NL [LC171402]), as well as more distantly related viruses, including Powassan virus (POWV; NC_003687.1), Langat virus (LGTV; NC_003690.1), and Louping-ill virus (LIV; Y07863.1). The resulting identity values were visualized as a heatmap (Figure B), revealing high conservation within the broader TBEV group, with pairwise identities generally exceeding 92%. In contrast, interspecies comparisons showed substantially lower identity values, with Powassan virus sharing only ∼74–77% identity and Langat virus sharing 81–83% identity with TBEV strains, consistent with their divergent evolutionary trajectories.In contrast, the envelope (E) protein, which mediates host cell entry and serves as a major antigenic determinant, exhibited less pronounced subtype-specific divergence (Figure C). Within the TBEV group, E protein identities ranged from 94% to 100%. Notably, Hypr and Vasilchenko shared 100% identity, indicating limited sequence divergence. Sofjin, Zausaev, and Baikalian exhibited similarly high levels of conservation. Comparisons with more distantly related orthoflaviviruses, such as Powassan virus and Langat virus, revealed lower E protein identities (77–88%), in line with their antigenic profiles. Collectively, these data suggest that whilst both NS1 and E proteins are conserved across TBEV, NS1 may be subject to distinct selective pressures, potentially reflecting differences in functional constraints linked to pathogenicity.Structural Comparison of NS1 across Orthoflavivirus Strains Reveals Lineage- and Pathogenicity-Specific DifferencesTo investigate the structural basis underlying the differences in pathogenicity and vector specificity among orthoflaviviruses, we performed a comparative structural analysis of NS1 from representative tick-borne (TBEV) and mosquito-borne (ZIKV, JEV, and WNV) viruses. We focused on identifying lineage-specific amino acid (AA) differences and structural features that may correlate with pathogenic potential and tick- or mosquito-vector tropism.Similar to other orthoflaviviruses, the NS1 protein of TBEV comprises three distinct domains: a β-roll (residues 1–29), a wing domain (residues 38–180), and a β-ladder domain (residues 181–352) (Figure A). , High-resolution structural alignment of NS1 monomers from the TBEV-Vs (low-pathogenic) and -Hypr (high-pathogenic) strains revealed several discrete (22 AA) substitutions, particularly localized in the surface-exposed wing domain (9 AA) and the distal β-ladder (13 AA) domain (Figure A, Supplementary Table S1). This domain clustering, with no AA changes in either the β-roll or connector regions, may contribute to the differences in neurovirulence observed between these strains.3Localization of sequence changes in representative low- and high-pathogenic strains of TBEV (A), ZIKA (B), JEV (C), and WNV (D) NS1. Domains are color coded as in Figure A. Initial atomic positions were based on (PDB ID: 4OIG) for all. (A) Positions of 22-AA changes in the three-dimensional structure of the Vs (low-path)- and Hypr (high-path)- NS1 monomer shown by AlphaFold3 and visualized in PyMOL. A focused view of the mutations in the Wing (yellow) and β-ladder (Pink) domains is indicated. Mutated amino acids are shown as an atomic stick representation. (B–D) NS1 of high- and low-pathogenic strains are indicated left and right, respectively. Domains are color coded as in Figure A. (B) Dimer of Asian (PDB: 5GS6) (left) and African (PDB: 5K6K) ZIKA (right) virus NS1, showing all 9 AA changes (orange). (C) Dimer of JEV genotype III- and genotype I-NS1 with 13 site-specific amino acid changes highlighted in orange. (D) NS1 dimer of lineage 1a- and lineage 2-WNV NS1, indicating 30 site-specific amino acid mutations.In Mosquito-borne ZIKV virus lineages linked to variable neurovirulence, NS1 structures exhibited lineage-specific changes at 9 AA. Comparison of NS1 monomers from Asian lineage (Brazil strain) and African lineage (Uganda strain) ZIKV isolates revealed AA changes in the central β-roll (1 AA), β-ladder (5 AA), and wing (3 AA) domain (Figure B, Supplementary Table S1). Of note, whilst the overall NS1 architecture is conserved, the Asian lineage is historically epidemiologically linked to congenital Zika syndrome, − whereas African strains may cause fatal pathogenicity. Whilst the overall NS1 architecture is conserved, three AA changes in the surface-exposed Wing domain have not been investigated in the context of pathogenic outcomes. Together, this suggests that minor structural remodeling in the NS1 surface may underlie differences in tissue tropism and pathogenesis.Structural variation in JEV NS1 from Genotype III (the highly pathogenic P20778 strain) and Genotype I (strain K94P05) exhibits conserved tertiary structures with 13 genotype-specific AA differences in the connector 2 loop (1 AA), the wing domain (4 AA), and the β-ladder (8 AA) (Figure C). These residues are positioned in proximity to putative glycosylation and oligomerization sites (Supplementary Table S1), potentially influencing NS1 dimerization or host immune interactions. Given that genotype I strains have displaced genotype III in several endemic regions, these may be related to transmissibility or immune escape. NS1 from WNV lineages show progressive changes within 29 AA, associated with high- and low-pathogenic strains. Structural comparison of NS1 from WNV Lineage 1a (highly pathogenic) and Lineage 2 (historically low-pathogenic, now emerging) revealed high conservation, with AA substitutions in each domain. The highest number was in the surface-exposed (wing) domain (11 AA). A total of 12 AA changes were in the β-ladder (Figure D). Notably, Lineage 2 NS1 exhibits substitutions in regions linked to lipid binding and ER membrane association, possibly linked with recent observations of increased neuroinvasive potential in clinical cases. These findings are consistent with the hypothesis that the evolution of NS1 within Lineage 2 may contribute to differences in its pathogenicity. Powassan virus is a tick-borne arbovirus endemic to North America. Comparison of Lineages 1 and 2 showed differences in NS1 sequences at only 1 AA in the β-roll (Phenylalanine [F] to Leucine [L] at position 247) (Supplementary Table S1).These comparative structural analyses demonstrate that lineage- and strain-specific residues in NS1 cluster in functionally important domains across both tick- and mosquito-borne orthoflaviviruses. Substitutions at these regions may influence protein-cell membrane interactions, potentially contributing to differences in virulence and vector specificity, particularly in emerging strains with altered clinical outcomes. Moreover, these observations are based on sequence and structural analysis and provide a framework for future experimental investigation of the proposed functional effects.TBEV NS1 Interacts with Tight Junction Proteins in a Strain-Specific MannerGiven the established role of related arbovirus NS1 in disrupting endothelial integrity, we next investigated whether TBEV NS1 interacts with key TJPs, including JAM-A, JAM-B, JAM-C, claudin-5, and claudin-10. Structural predictions using AlphaFold3-multimer models were performed for both high- (Hypr) and low-pathogenic (Vs) NS1 variants, focusing on the extracellular domains (ectodomains) of the TJPs, which represent the biologically accessible interfaces for secreted or membrane-associated NS1.
