full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionDespite the high conservation of orthoflavivirus NS1 across both tick-borne and mosquito-borne members, emerging evidence suggests divergent functional roles during pathogenesis shaped by vector lineage, host tropism, and strain-specific viral factors. ,,,,,− This study provides mechanistic insight into how NS1 interactions could relate to strain-specific disruption of the endothelial barrier in TBEV, focusing on NS1 interactions with BBB TJs. A key finding is the direct binding observed between NS1 from the neurovirulent Hypr strain and the adhesion molecule JAM-A, which was not the case for the low-virulence Vs strain. This differential binding was validated using biochemical (ELISA) and immunofluorescence assays (Figure ) in physiologically relevant brain microvascular endothelial hCMEC/3D cells that represent a model of the human BBB. Given that JAM-A has an established role in maintaining BBB integrity and regulating immune cell transmigration, , its engagement by Hypr NS1 may contribute to paracellular permeability and endothelial destabilization. This points to a targeted mechanism of BBB disruption, distinct from the generalized vascular leakage observed in mosquito-borne DENV and ZIKV, in which NS1 induces endothelial dysfunction through pattern-recognition receptor activation (e.g., TLR4) or complement pathways. , Unlike DENV NS1, which interacts with ZO-1 and claudins to broadly destabilize endothelial junctions, TBEV NS1 appeared to selectively engage claudins as indicated by the in silico AF3 model (Figure ). This suggests that BBB disruption in tick-borne orthoflaviviruses may rely on precise modulation of the endothelial interfaces critical for CNS entry, as opposed to pan-junctional disassembly. Our data also raise the intriguing hypothesis that the Hypr NS1–JAM-A interaction may be involved in neuroinvasion. Whether this represents a causal gateway or a consequence of systemic vascular damage, however, remains to be determined.Structurally, NS1 is a conserved dimer/trimer comprising β-roll, wing, and β-ladder domains. , Comparative analyses revealed that the 22 AA differences between Hypr and Vs NS1 localize to the wing and β-ladder domains implicated in host membrane interactions and immune modulation. For other orthoflaviviruses, these domains mediate lipid binding, immune complex formation, and cell surface anchorage. , The clustering of strain-specific substitutions in these surface-exposed regions may support a model in which minor sequence variations may reshape host interaction profiles, in the absence of altering the architecture of NS1.This concept aligns with the broader patterns observed during orthoflavivirus evolution. For example, minor substitutions in NS1 from ZIKV (Asian vs African lineages) or WNV (lineage 1 vs 2) are sufficient to alter neurotropism, likely via changes in host protein or membrane interactions. , Our findings suggest similar adaptive pressures for tick-borne orthoflaviviruses, where subtle NS1 modifications may fine-tune endothelial engagement and influence the neuroinvasive potential.The absence of JAM-A binding by Vs-NS1 underscores the existence of alternative CNS entry mechanisms. Although Vs is less neurovirulent in murine models, human infections can result in persistent neurological symptoms and chronic inflammation. , This suggests that Vs pathogenesis may involve more gradual neuroinvasiveness via mechanisms that do not require direct NS1-JAM-A interactions (e.g., immune cell trafficking or inflammation-induced paracellular leak).Interestingly, our AF3 model predicted that Vs NS1 exhibits modest binding to Claudin-5 and Hypr NS1 to Claudin-10, key components of BBB tight junctions responsible for regulating paracellular ion flux and maintaining endothelial barrier integrity. , The physiological relevance of these interactions and the potential involvement of post-translational modifications such as glycosylation in their regulation, remains unknown. Claudin extracellular loops are short and structurally constrained. Direct NS1–claudin interactions have not been demonstrated in vivo. It is more plausible that claudin disassembly during TBEV infection results from cytokine-driven inflammatory signaling, as observed in DENV where NS1 triggers TLR4-mediated endothelial activation and downstream production of TNF-α and IL-6, leading to tight junction destabilization. ZIKA NS1 has been shown to suppress Claudin-5 expression in human brain microvascular endothelial cells, contributing to BBB breakdown. Although that study did not assess direct NS1–Claudin-5 binding, our AF3 multimer modeling predicted moderate binding of both African- and Asian-lineage NS1 proteins to Claudin-5 (Figure D–E and Table and Supplementary Table S5; ipTM = 0.76), consistent with strains previously associated with BBB disruption. ,, Furthermore, AF3 predicted distinct claudin-binding profiles for Hypr NS1 and Vs NS1, and their interaction networks also differed substantially. The Hypr NS1–Claudin-10 complex exhibited 12 predicted contacts, compared with 7 for the Vs NS1–Claudin-5 complex (Supplementary Table S3). Similar strain-dependent differences were observed in ZIKV NS1 models (Supplementary Table S5), despite large conservation of their interface residues. These observations suggest that variation in the extent and stability of protein–protein interactions may contribute to strain-specific binding properties, although experimental validation is required to substantiate this conclusion.In line with this study, a recent study demonstrated NS1-TNF-α-mediated increased endothelial permeability in TBEV-infected human lung microvascular endothelial cells. Direct NS1–TJP interactions were not investigated, and only the Far Eastern subtype Sofjin strain was studied, limiting mechanistic comparison. The findings were, however, consistent with our data and suggest that NS1-mediated pathogenicity may be regulated by multiple strain-specific mechanisms, enabling differential clinical outcomes. Similar phenomena have been reported for other neurotropic viruses, such as JEV, where cytokine-mediated modulation of claudins as opposed to direct virus protein binding, appears to drive changes in BBB permeability. In summary, we present evidence from predictive modeling and in vitro binding assays suggesting that TBEV NS1 may engage endothelial junction proteins, particularly JAM-A, in a strain-specific manner. Through the integration of computational structural predictions, evolutionary sequence analysis, and in vitro validation, we offer a framework to compare viruses with differential pathogenesis. While claudins also represent key TJPs identified as potential NS1 binders in silico, Claudin-5 and Claudin-10 are predominantly localized within intercellular junction complexes, which can limit their accessibility in vitro. Future studies will investigate their role in conjunction with the in vivo mechanisms of NS1-mediated junction disruption to assess how naturally occurring mutations influence these interactions in emerging strains. Given the expanding geographical range of both tick- and mosquito-borne orthoflaviviruses driven by climate change, − monitoring NS1 sequence evolution may provide early indicators of shifts in virulence or transmission potential, informing diagnostic development and vaccine design.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionOrthoflaviviruses, an important genus within the Flaviviridae family, include medically significant mosquito- and tick-borne viruses such as dengue (DENV), West Nile (WNV), Zika (ZIKV), and tick-borne encephalitis viruses. All share structural and pathogenic features and cause a wide spectrum of clinical outcomes in humans ranging from asymptomatic infections to severe, sometimes fatal disease. Severe flavivirus infections are associated with systemic vascular leakage, hemorrhagic manifestations, or encephalitic pathology, − often involving breach or compromise of the blood–brain barrier (BBB). − The orthoflavivirus genome encodes three structural proteins (C, prM/M, and E) and seven nonstructural (NS) proteins (NS1, NS2A, NS2B, NS3, NS4A, NS4B, and NS5). NS1 is a structurally conserved and critical virulence factor encoded by orthoflaviviruses, including TBEV. It is a glycoprotein that exists in multiple forms, intracellular, membrane-associated, and secreted, which circulates in the host bloodstream (Figure A)all of which contribute to virus replication, immune evasion, and pathogenesis. − 1Cryo-EM structure of orthoflavivirus non-structural protein 1 (NS1). (A) The NS1 dimer is shown in cartoon representation. The ribbon diagram highlights the β-roll, wing, β-ladder, and connector domains (1 and 2), colored blue, yellow, pink, green, and purple, respectively, in a single monomer. Dengue virus (DENV) NS1 dimer (PDB ID: 4OIG) is shown interacting with a phospholipid membrane. Percentage identity matrices for NS1 (B) or (C) (envelop) E proteins are indicated among 14 tick-borne orthoflaviviruses (TBFV), generated by ClustalW. Each matrix represents the percentage of identical residues between each pair of sequences in the alignment. Identity values are shown as an inferno heatmap with a gradient from highest (light yellow; 100%) to lowest (dark purple; 74%).Extensive work in mosquito-borne orthoflaviviruses, particularly DENV, yellow fever virus (YFV), and ZIKV, demonstrates that secreted NS1 directly perturbs endothelial barrier integrity by engaging glycocalyx-associated molecules, inducing hyperpermeability, and disrupting tight junction protein (TJP) architecture through complement activation, inflammatory signaling, and direct endothelial binding. − These studies collectively show that NS1 functions as a soluble pathogenic effector capable of driving vascular dysfunction independently of viral replication and highlight its capacity to remodel endothelial surfaces, destabilize intercellular junctions, and facilitate barrier breakdown. , In contrast to the depth of mechanistic insight available for mosquito-borne orthoflaviruses, the role of NS1 in tick-borne arbovirus biology remains comparatively underexplored. full_text_excerpt: AbstractTick-borne encephalitis virus (TBEV) invades the central nervous system (CNS) through strain-specific mechanisms that remain poorly understood. For mosquito-borne orthoflaviviruses such as dengue and yellow fever viruses, the nonstructural protein 1 (NS1) has been shown to disrupt endothelial barrier integrity by targeting tight junction proteins (TJPs), facilitating viral neuroinvasion. However, comparable mechanisms in TBEVs remain largely unexplored. Here, we investigated the potential interaction of NS1 from high (Hypr)- and low (Vs)-pathogenic TBEV strains with different blood–brain barrier (BBB) TJPs, using AlphaFold3 (AF3) multimer modeling and in vitro binding assays. AF3 modeling suggested that NS1 from the highly pathogenic strain may interact with multiple TJPs, including junctional adhesion molecule A (JAM-A), a key component of the paracellular barrier. In contrast, the low-pathogenic Vs showed a more restricted interaction profile. Experimental validation using recombinant NS1 proteins revealed strain-specific binding profiles: Hypr NS1 displayed high-affinity, saturable direct binding to immobilized JAM-A (KD,app = 0.81 nM), whereas Vs NS1 showed no binding. Immunofluorescence assays on human lung epithelial (A549) and BBB (hCMEC/D3) cells further demonstrated colocalization between Hypr NS1 and JAM-A, supporting a potential interaction. No direct binding to ZO-1, a barrier scaffold lacking an extracellular domain, was observed for either strain. This differential interaction profile may be modulated by 22 amino acids localized to the Wing and β-Ladder domains within NS1, which distinguish Hypr from Vs. full_text: Synergistic Effects of Behavioral Feedback and Seasonality Generate Chaos in Cooperative Multi-Pathogen Systems Rodrigo Amaral Lind1, Fakhteh Ghanbarnejad2, and Seba Contreras3,4* 1Institute for the Dynamics of Complex Systems, University of Göttingen, Göttingen, Germany. 2School of Technology and Architecture, SRH University of Applied Sciences Heidelberg, Leipzig Campus, Germany 3Hangzhou International Innovation Institute, Beihang University, Hangzhou, China. 4Interdisciplinary Center for the Mathematical Modeling of Infectious Disease Dynamics (IMMIDD), University of Münster, Münster, Germany. * Corresponding Author: Seba Contreras (contreras@buaa.edu.cn) Abstract Infectious diseases may interact by competing for the same hosts or by facilitating subsequent infections. Understanding the dynamics of such multi-pathogen systems, particularly those subject to endemic seasonality and mitigation, is essential for designing robust public health interventions. We propose a three-stage modeling framework to disentangle the interplay between seasonality and behavioral feedback as a way of mitigation. First, we analyze a coupled susceptible-infectious-recovered-susceptible (SIRS) system without external forcing and show that the abrupt transition between the disease-free and endemic equilibria arises from a backward bifurcation-induced first-order phase transition. Second, we independently examine seasonality and behavioral feedback, characterizing where and when oscillatory behavior is induced near critical tipping points. Third, we demonstrate that their combination generates complex multi-annual wave patterns, with high-incidence cycles driven by seasonality and low-incidence intervals driven by behavioral feedback. By mapping stability as a function of seasonal forcing, mitigation strength, and cooperativity, we identify distinct period-doubling cascades with chaotic signatures arising from different mechanisms: the interplay between seasonality and behavior, and inter-pathogen cooperativity with the backward bifurcation it induces. We then analyze how these mechanisms interact across parameter ranges. Altogether, we show that cooperation fundamentally expands the spectrum of possible epidemic patterns, highlighting the importance of considering multi-pathogen interactions in epidemic modeling and control strategies. 1 arXiv:2609.07015v1 [q-bio.PE] 7 Sep 2026 1 Introduction Emergent and re-emergent infectious diseases can severely disrupt societal function and well-being. Whether an outbreak permeates large fractions of the population depends on the interplay between pathogen and host population, modulated by internal and external forces. Key mechanisms include societal self-regulation via information feedback loops [1–5] and seasonality [6–8]. These factors induce complex dynamics in both epidemic and endemic states [9–11]. However, diseases rarely occur in isolation: pathogens spread simultaneously and interact through varying degrees of competition or cooperation [12]. While competition, driven by mechanisms such as cross-immunity, active mitigation, or depletion of the susceptible pool, is well documented [13–15], pathogen cooperation presents distinct modeling challenges. In this regime, one pathogen facilitates co-infection or subsequent infection with another, often by compromising physiological barriers or suppressing immune responses. For instance, some influenza viruses damage the respiratory epithelium, increasing susceptibility to secondary bacterial infections [16–18]. Similar facilitation is observed in HIV and hepatitis C co-infections [19–21], among human papillomavirus (HPV) types [22], in bacterial co-infections associated with SARS-CoV-2 [23], and in the mutual enhancement between influenza and invasive pneumococcal disease [24–26]. However, the coupling between infections and interventions can also be behavioral: due to risk compensation [27], interventions against HIV can also facilitate the spread of other sexually transmitted infections [28,29]. Mechanistically, multipathogen interaction has been modeled at varying complexity, from sequential coupling [30,31] to systems incorporating full interactions and all possible disease states [32,33]. The competition-cooperation spectrum can be abstracted into a single coupling parameter C, which modulates the force of infection during co-infection. Here, C > 1 indicates cooperation, while C < 1 implies competition [33]. In a symmetric susceptible- infectious-removed (SIR), SIR-SIR setting, [33–35] identified an "explosive" acceleration of contagion when C ≥2. Even for overall reproduction numbers below one, this interaction drives a phenomenon resembling a first-order phase transition, explained by a positive feedback loop between existing and new infections. In models with waning immunity, such transitions often arise from the system tipping across the boundaries of attractor basins, typically via a backward bifurcation. Mechanisms known to induce such bifurcations include exogenous reinfection (e.g., tuberculosis) [36–38], superinfection [39], relapse [40], imperfect vaccination [41–43], population heterogeneity [44], and antibody-dependent enhancement (as in dengue virus) [30,31]. In this paper, building on the multi-pathogen SIR-SIR configuration of [33–35], we investigate the interplay between waning immunity, behavioral feedback, and seasonality in a SIRS coinfection model, proceeding in three stages. First, we examine the SIRS-SIRS model without external forcing and show that the first-order phase transition persists and is amplified: for reproduction numbers below one, a bistable region emerges in which a backward bifurcation drives the transition between the disease-free equilibrium (DFE) and the endemic equilibrium (EE). Second, introducing mitigation through behavioral feedback and seasonality individually, we find that each can generate limit cycles near the tipping point. Finally, we map the stability of the full system as a function of seasonal forcing and mitigation strength, revealing period-doubling cascades to chaos and alternating wave regimes around the critical reproduction number: one driven by seasonality (high incidence, fast dynamics) and the other by mitigation (low incidence, slow dynamics). 2 Methods 2.1 Model backbone We use a compartmental model to describe the simultaneous spread of two pathogens within a single population, accounting for waning immunity and mechanisms of interaction among pathogens (competition-cooperation [33,34]), society (behavioral feedback [1,5]), and the environment (seasonality [2]). First, we examine the SIRS-SIRS model without external forcing and show that the first-order phase transition persists and is amplified: for reproduction numbers below one, a bistable region emerges in which a backward bifurcation drives the transition between the disease-free equilibrium (DFE) and the endemic equilibrium (EE). Second, introducing mitigation through behavioral feedback and seasonality individually, we find that each can generate limit cycles near the tipping point. Finally, we map the stability of the full system as a function of seasonal forcing and mitigation strength, revealing period-doubling cascades to chaos and alternating wave regimes around the critical reproduction number: one driven by seasonality (high incidence, fast dynamics) and the other by mitigation (low incidence, slow dynamics). 2 Methods 2.1 Model backbone We use a compartmental model to describe the simultaneous spread of two pathogens within a single population, accounting for waning immunity and mechanisms of interaction among pathogens (competition-cooperation [33,34]), society (behavioral feedback [1,5]), and the environment (seasonality [2]). The model follows a susceptible-infectious- recovered-susceptible (SIRS) architecture with full interaction between the two pathogens, yielding 9 compartments (see Figure 1).
